classification_signals: Abstract: 'We offer a theory to help understand and explain these effects.'
Section 1: 'Introduction.' sets the stage for a conceptual argument.
Section 2: 'Biologically-based design.' synthesizes existing research to build a theoretical foundation.
Section 3: 'Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment.' develops the core theoretical argument.
Section 5: 'Three different conceptions of being human.' introduces a conceptual framework for human nature.

Appendix I: 'Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.' presents practical techniques derived from the theoretical framework, stating 'They are the outcome of a theoretical and scientific methodology that is too voluminous to be reviewed here.' (p. 24)
Extensive citation of other research (e.g., Alexander, Salingaros, Ulrich, Kellert) to support theoretical claims, rather than presenting new data.
title: Neuroscience, the Natural Environment, and Building Design.

findings.antecedent: Human mind
findings.consequent: Split between genetically-structured neural systems and internally-generated worldview
findings.source: Abstract
findings.quote: The human mind is split between genetically-structured neural systems, and an internally-generated worldview.

findings.antecedent: Contemporary architects imposing artificial meaning on built environment (contradicting physical and natural processes)
findings.consequent: Buildings and cities inhuman in form, scale, and construction
findings.source: Abstract
findings.quote: By imposing an artificial meaning on the built environment, contemporary architects contradict physical and natural processes, and thus create buildings and cities that are inhuman in their form, scale, and construction.

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design (incorporating organic life into the built environment)
findings.consequent: Reconnection of human beings to the buildings and places they inhabit
findings.source: Abstract
findings.quote: Biophilic design, as one of the most recent and viable reconnection theories, incorporates organic life into the built environment in an essential manner.

findings.antecedent: Building forms, articulations, and textures following the same geometry found in all living forms
findings.source: Abstract
findings.quote: Extending this logic, the building forms, articulations, and textures could themselves follow the same geometry found in all living forms.

findings.antecedent: Designs which connect humans to the lived experience
findings.consequent: Overall sense of wellbeing, positive and therapeutic consequences on physiology
findings.source: Abstract
findings.quote: Empirical evidence confirms that designs which connect humans to the lived experience enhance our overall sense of wellbeing, with positive and therapeutic consequences on physiology.

findings.antecedent: Informational fields present in the natural environment
findings.source: 1. Introduction.
findings.quote: the end result of the evolution of our neural system in response to external stimuli such as the informational fields present in the natural environment.

findings.antecedent: Information field (from environment)
findings.consequent: Neurological mechanism reaction, physiological reaction (body state)
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design.
findings.quote: Our neurological mechanism reacts to the information field (the transmission component), while inducing a reaction in the state of our body (the physiological component).

findings.antecedent: Intrinsic qualities of natural and built environments
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design.
findings.quote: Both natural and built environments possess intrinsic qualities that enable such a strong connection, and which in turn can be healing.

findings.antecedent: Natural environment
findings.consequent: Shaping of human bodies and senses
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design.
findings.quote: What we are depends on the natural environment that shaped our bodies and senses (Kellert, 2005; Kellert & Wilson, 1993; Orians & Heerwagen, 1992).

findings.antecedent: Determinant qualities in the environment
findings.consequent: Human existence, sense of belonging and wellbeing
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design.
findings.quote: We thus depend on the presence of certain determinant qualities in the environment not only for our existence, but equally for our sense of belonging and wellbeing.

findings.antecedent: Certain types of environmental information
findings.consequent: Neurological nourishment, activation of brain's pleasure centers, reduction of pain
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design.
findings.quote: Humans have an innate hunger for certain types of information: the circuits for this have been associated with the brain's pleasure centers, which also control the reduction of pain (Biederman & Vessel, 2006).

findings.antecedent: Fractal qualities (ordered details, nested scaling hierarchy) in environment
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design.
findings.quote: fractal qualities in our environment (i.e., ordered details arranged in a nested scaling hierarchy) contribute positively to human wellbeing (Hagerhall, Purcell & Taylor, 2004; Taylor, 2006; Taylor et. al., 2005).

findings.antecedent: Built fractal patterns
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design.
findings.quote: The parallel between built fractal patterns and possible cerebral organization is too strong to be a coincidence (Salingaros, 2006).

findings.antecedent: Natural environments (or artificial environments mimicking natural geometry)
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design.
findings.quote: undisputed clinical advantages (faster hospital healing) of natural environments, including artificial environments mimicking geometrical qualities of natural environments (Frumkin, 2001; Ulrich, 1984; 2000).

findings.antecedent: Viewing natural (or videos of natural) environments
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design.
findings.quote: Pain relief in hospital settings is significantly improved by viewing natural (or videos of natural) environments (Tse et. al., 2002), thus confirming the link between specific types of informational input and pain reduction.

findings.antecedent: Neurologically-nourishing environment (visual complexity, highest organized complexity)
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design.
findings.quote: Reaction to a neurologically-nourishing environment is physiological (i.e. emotional) rather than intellectual. There is mounting evidence of an innate information-processing system that has evolved along with the rest of our physiology (Joye, 2006; 2007a; 2007b). This system is acutely tuned to the visual complexity of the natural environment, specifically to respond positively to the highest levels of organized complexity (Salingaros, 2006).

findings.antecedent: Geometrical properties of natural/biological forms (beyond fractals, including hierarchy of subsymmetries)
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design.
findings.quote: Additional geometrical properties of natural/biological forms clearly contribute to a positive physiological response in humans (Alexander, 2002-2005; Enquist & Arak, 1994; Kellert, 2005; Klinger & Salingaros, 2000; Salingaros, 2005; 2006). Symmetry more precisely, a hierarchy of subsymmetries on many distinct scales plays a crucial role.

findings.antecedent: Organized information (in environment)
findings.consequent: Positive or negative effect on perceptive system
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design.
findings.quote: Not only the presence of information, but especially how that information is organized, produces a positive or negative effect on our perceptive system (Klinger & Salingaros, 2000; Salingaros, 2006).

findings.antecedent: Ordered geometry of biological forms
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design.
findings.quote: We assume an underlying genetic factor as the basis for why the ordered geometry of biological forms connects with and leads to healing effects on human beings.

findings.antecedent: Built environment following informational template of life forms
findings.consequent: Better fit with intrinsic human complexity
findings.source: 2. Biologically-based design.
findings.quote: The built environment, considered as an externalization of intrinsic human complexity fits better in the larger scheme of things whenever it follows the same informational template.

findings.antecedent: Structures embodying organized complexity
findings.consequent: Stronger physiological and psychological connection in human beings (compared to plain or disorganized environments)
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: Human beings connect physiologically and psychologically to structures embodying organized complexity more strongly than to environments that are either too plain, or which present disorganized complexity (Salingaros, 2006).

findings.antecedent: Connection process (with environment)
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: The connection process (outlined in the following sections) plays a key role in our lives, because it influences our health and mental wellbeing.

findings.antecedent: Contact with nature and complex geometry of natural forms
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: Wilson's Biophilia Hypothesis asserts that we need contact with nature, and with the complex geometry of natural forms, just as much as we require nutrients and air for our metabolism (Kellert, 2005; Kellert & Wilson, 1993).

findings.antecedent: Artificial representation of nature (lacking requisite complexity)
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: While many architects may indeed claim to practice in this way, they more frequently replace nature by a very poor image of nature: an artificial representation or substitute that lacks the requisite complexity.

findings.antecedent: Interacting plants (ecological and visual complexity)
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: Nature exhibits ecological complexity: interacting plants that in turn provide visual complexity, which is a source of neurological nourishment.

findings.antecedent: Biophilic thinking (respect for nature)
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: Sustainability goes hand-in-hand with a new respect for nature coming from biophilia (Kellert, 2005).

findings.antecedent: Industrial building-plus-garden (armature hostile to human sensibilities)
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: The natural aspect of an industrial building-plus-garden is simply a biological component grafted onto an armature that is fundamentally hostile to human sensibilities. It still triggers an underlying neurological disconnection on a basic level.

findings.antecedent: Biophilic architecture (incorporating essential geometrical qualities of nature, complex built geometry)
findings.consequent: Deeper human connection to built environment
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: A second, and much deeper aspect of biophilic architecture requires us to incorporate the essential geometrical qualities of nature into the building and urban structure. This implies a more complex built geometry, following the same complexity as natural forms themselves.

findings.antecedent: Engagement with information and its organization (in environment)
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: Neurological nourishment depends upon an engagement with information and its organization.

findings.antecedent: Traditional ornamentation, color, articulated surfaces, and interior space shape
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: Traditional ornamentation, color, articulated surfaces, and the shape of interior space helped to achieve informational connectivity.

findings.antecedent: Ornamentation (distillation of geometrical connective rules)
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: ornamentation in its deepest expressions is far more than that: it is a distillation of geometrical connective rules that trigger our neurophysiology directly.

findings.antecedent: Underlying geometrical complexity of living structure (in organisms, artifacts, and buildings)
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: the underlying geometrical complexity of living structure is what nourishes humans. This geometry could be equally expressed in biological organisms as in artifacts and buildings: the difference is merely one of degree (Alexander, 2002-2005).

findings.antecedent: Living forms and their embodied geometrical characteristics
findings.source: 3. Biophilic architecture and neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: Living forms and the geometrical characteristics they embody must be protected from destruction, because they provide us with neurological nourishment (Wilson, 1984).

findings.antecedent: Desire to overcome nature (20th-century architecture)
findings.consequent: Separation of man from universe, autonomous architectural order
findings.source: 4. An architecture that arises from human nature.
findings.quote: The desire to overcome nature, to separate man from the universe by placing him above natural constraints, led to the ultimate architectural assertion of the twentieth century, one expressing total autonomy.

findings.antecedent: 20th-century architecture (separation from the world)
findings.consequent: Value predicated on degree of separation
findings.source: 4. An architecture that arises from human nature.
findings.quote: the value of twentieth-century architecture was now solely predicated on its degree of separation from the world around it: the world in which humans seek comfort and shelter (Masden, 2006).

findings.antecedent: Ideology
findings.consequent: Control of human actions (violating biological nature)
findings.source: 4. An architecture that arises from human nature.
findings.quote: People are sometimes manipulated into adopting an ideology, which then controls their actions in violation of their biological nature (Salingaros, 2004).

findings.antecedent: Abstract, mechanical world
findings.consequent: Minimal human interaction with natural world, disconnection
findings.source: 5. Three different conceptions of being human.
findings.quote: In the first level, a human being is regarded as a component placed into an abstract, mechanical world. Here, human beings interact only minimally (superficially) with the natural world, a condition of being disconnected.

findings.antecedent: Biological human being (with sensors)
findings.source: 5. Three different conceptions of being human.
findings.quote: Here, humans are biological entities: animals that possess a sensory apparatus enabling them to receive and use measurable input. This is a condition of biological connectedness to the world, i.e. situatedness (Salingaros & Masden, 2006a).

findings.antecedent: Transcendent human being (spiritual)
findings.source: 5. Three different conceptions of being human.
findings.quote: The third conception corresponds to the much older metaphysical picture of humans as spiritual beings, connected to the universe in ways that other animals are not. This is a condition of transcendental engagement with the world.

findings.antecedent: Past decades and centuries
findings.consequent: Regression in depth of human connection to surroundings (universe)
findings.source: 5. Three different conceptions of being human.
findings.quote: humankind has regressed in the depth of its connection to its surroundings (i.e. the universe) over the past decades and centuries.

findings.antecedent: Cartesian method
findings.consequent: Detachment from our world (for scientific enquiry)
findings.source: 5. Three different conceptions of being human.
findings.quote: the Cartesian method required us to detach ourselves from our world in the name of scientific enquiry, in order to be able to perform unbiased experiments.

findings.antecedent: Industrialized world (machines, industrial materials, media images)
findings.consequent: Suppression of human connection to nature
findings.source: 6. Level one: the abstract human being.
findings.quote: people's connection to nature are suppressed. Modern individuals at least in the more developed countries live in a physical world defined by machines and industrial materials, and whose information fields come from media images and messages.

findings.antecedent: Disconnected population
findings.consequent: Insensitivity to the healing effects of natural environments
findings.source: 6. Level one: the abstract human being.
findings.quote: An automated, disconnected population is insensitive to the healing effects of natural environments.

findings.antecedent: Visually sterile, industrial 'look' (polished metal or porcelain surfaces)
findings.source: 6. Level one: the abstract human being.
findings.quote: A "healthy" environment became associated with a visually sterile, industrial "look" of polished metal or porcelain surfaces.

findings.antecedent: Preoccupation with improved health
findings.consequent: Suspicion of all life, exclusion of plants/animals from environment
findings.source: 6. Level one: the abstract human being.
findings.quote: People's preoccupation with improved health made them suspicious of all life, not just the harmful microbes and fungi that cause disease.

findings.antecedent: Psychological conditioning
findings.source: 6. Level one: the abstract human being.
findings.quote: This contemporary condition demonstrates that human beings can be psychologically conditioned to act against their biological nature (Hoffer, 1951; Salingaros, 2004).

findings.antecedent: Formal criteria and abstractions in architecture
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being.
findings.quote: That changed when formal criteria and abstractions were introduced, replacing those of an older, humanistic architecture.

findings.antecedent: Neurologically non-nourishing built environment
findings.consequent: Instinctive negative reaction, physical anxiety and distress
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being.
findings.quote: Therefore, we will instinctively react in a negative manner to a built environment that is neurologically non-nourishing, or which might actually cause physical anxiety and distress.

findings.antecedent: Geometry of the environment (hospital)
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being.
findings.quote: In hospital design, the geometry of the environment plays a significant role in how long it takes for a patient to be cured. Roger Ulrich has done pioneering work in this topic (Ulrich, 1984; 2000).

findings.antecedent: Symmetry, visual connections, ornament, and fine detail on buildings
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being.
findings.quote: Symmetry, visual connections, ornament, and fine detail are necessary on buildings; not for any stylistic reason, but because our perception is built to engage with those features (Enquist & Arak, 1994; Salingaros, 2003; 2006).

findings.antecedent: Environment eschewing natural/traditional visual elements
findings.consequent: Negative physiological consequences, negative mental health, decreased wellbeing
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being.
findings.quote: Creating an environment that deliberately eschews these elements (visual elements which are found in nature and in all traditional architectures) has negative consequences for our physiology, and thus for our mental health and sense of wellbeing (Joye, 2006; 2007a; 2007b; Kellert, 2005).

findings.antecedent: Environments devoid of neurologically-nourishing information (colorless, drab, minimalist surfaces and spaces)
findings.consequent: Mimicry of human pathology symptoms (macular degeneration, stroke, cerebral achromatopsia, visual agnosia), anxiety, sensation of sensory deprivation/neurophysiologic breakdown
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being.
findings.quote: Environments devoid of neurologically-nourishing information mimic signs of human pathology. For example, colorless, drab, minimalist surfaces and spaces reproduce clinical symptoms of macular degeneration, stroke, cerebral achromatopsia, and visual agnosia (Salingaros, 2003; 2006). We feel anxious in such environments, because they provoke in us a similar sensation as sensory deprivation and neurophysiologic breakdown.

findings.antecedent: Naturalistic and stimulating habitats (for zoo animals)
findings.consequent: Improved psychological and social well-being, normal/healthier behavior patterns (animals)
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being.
findings.quote: Judith Heerwagen has studied zoo animal behavior in naturalistic versus more artificial environments (Heerwagen, 2005)... As a consequence, the animals' psychological and social well-being has been drastically improved... Moved to more naturalistic and stimulating habitats, the animals returned to more normal, healthier behavior patterns.

findings.antecedent: Drab, monotonous, minimalist environments (for zoo animals)
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being.
findings.quote: Zoo animals kept in drab, monotonous, and minimalist environments (i.e. those that we humans also perceive as boring and depressing) exhibited neurotic, aberrant, and antisocial behavior never observed in the wild.

findings.antecedent: Complexity and stimulation in the environment
findings.consequent: Increased intelligence of a developing animal
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being.
findings.quote: Evidence has been accumulating since the 1960s that complexity and stimulation in the environment can lead to increased intelligence of a developing animal.

findings.antecedent: Information-rich environments (for young rats)
findings.consequent: Increased brain size, improved neural connectivity (up to 20%), better performance in intelligence tests/training
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being.
findings.quote: Incontrovertible results are obtained with young rats raised in information-rich environments, whose brains increase in size, and can improve their neural connectivity by up to 20% (Squire & Kandel, 1999: page 200)... Those rats raised in enriched environments are then observed to do much better in intelligence tests (such as solving complex maze problems) and training.

findings.antecedent: Room with hierarchical subdivisions and natural detail
findings.consequent: Marked physiological response (favorable), not always consciously recognized
findings.source: 7. Level two: the biological human being.
findings.quote: physiological monitors recorded a marked response in favor of the room with hierarchical subdivisions and natural detail (Tsunetsugu, Miyazaki & Sato, 2005). We (and the study's authors) conclude that physiological effects of the environment cannot always be consciously recognized.

findings.antecedent: Internalized complex environmental data (expert knowledge)
findings.source: 8. Extending level two: expert knowledge and patterns.
findings.quote: complex data about the environment have become so internalized that perception seems almost extrasensory (but is not).

findings.antecedent: Well-developed perceptual skills (expert knowledge)
findings.source: 8. Extending level two: expert knowledge and patterns.
findings.quote: Many qualities often attributed to intelligence are in fact the result of well-developed perceptual skills at the level of expert knowledge.

findings.antecedent: Environment and learning
findings.consequent: Shaping of neural network, acquisition of structural and functional pattern recognition
findings.source: 8. Extending level two: expert knowledge and patterns.
findings.quote: Our neural network is shaped by the environment and learning, thus acquiring additional, non-genetic properties. These properties include the recognition of structural and functional patterns.

findings.antecedent: Emotionally learned patterns (through perception)
findings.consequent: Action similar to inherited (genetically-based) responses, positive emotion (due to satisfying internal template)
findings.source: 8. Extending level two: expert knowledge and patterns.
findings.quote: Emotional learning is the result of sensory input, but remains subconscious (i.e. stored in nondeclarative memory)... Patterns learned emotionally through perception act in the same way as inherited (genetically-based) responses. The reason they evoke a positive emotion to begin with, is because they satisfy an internal template.

findings.antecedent: Patterns (body language, environmental cues, ornamentation)
findings.consequent: Sense-making of social importance, 'sixth sense' for social interaction
findings.source: 8. Extending level two: expert knowledge and patterns.
findings.quote: Patterns also can help us make sense of the social importance of our body language... and which I imagine we cue against our environment (which is why ornamentation may be very important).

findings.antecedent: Patterns recognized by neurophysiologic apparatus
findings.consequent: Understanding humanity and its connection to the universe
findings.source: 8. Extending level two: expert knowledge and patterns.
findings.quote: Patterns recognized by our neurophysiologic apparatus are a key to understanding humanity and its connection to the universe.

findings.antecedent: Patterns in human activity
findings.consequent: Generation of forms and connective complexity in traditional architecture and urbanism
findings.source: 8. Extending level two: expert knowledge and patterns.
findings.quote: Almost every human activity will be found to contain patterns, and those patterns generate the forms and connective complexity of traditional architecture and urbanism (Alexander et. al., 1977).

findings.antecedent: Increasing complexity of interaction (neurophysiologically detectable)
findings.source: 9. Further extending level two: human-machine and human-animal interactions.
findings.quote: Increasing the complexity of interaction in a definite direction (defined precisely by what our neurophysiology and sensory apparatus are built to detect) eventually leads to higher degrees of human connectivity.

findings.antecedent: Contact with domestic animals
findings.source: 9. Further extending level two: human-machine and human-animal interactions.
findings.quote: people have benefited from (and documented) the positive emotional and health effects of contact with domestic animals.

findings.antecedent: Human-animal interactions
findings.consequent: Positive physiological and psychological effects (via information exchange)
findings.source: 9. Further extending level two: human-machine and human-animal interactions.
findings.quote: Whatever positive physiological and psychological effects are observed to result from human-animal interactions, they must certainly occur via information exchange.

findings.antecedent: Complex, organized informational patterns (evolved with human body)
findings.source: 9. Further extending level two: human-machine and human-animal interactions.
findings.quote: What makes us recognizably human is a set of complex, organized informational patterns that evolved along with our body.

findings.antecedent: Abstract forms of architecture
findings.source: 9. Further extending level two: human-machine and human-animal interactions.
findings.quote: The processes at work in our neurological hardware require a far greater degree of information than the abstract forms of architecture currently provide.

findings.antecedent: Wilson's work
findings.consequent: Biological basis for supernatural aspects of human nature
findings.source: 10. Level three: the transcendent human being.
findings.quote: Wilson has made remarkable progress in providing a biological basis for what was previously attributed to the supernatural aspects of human nature (Wilson, 1978; 1984).

findings.antecedent: Beginning of modern (industrial) times
findings.consequent: Dismissal of neurological nourishment and engagement mechanism
findings.source: 10. Level three: the transcendent human being.
findings.quote: the mechanism of neurological nourishment and engagement was dismissed at the beginning of modern (industrial) times.

findings.antecedent: Fundamental geometrical properties
findings.source: 10. Level three: the transcendent human being.
findings.quote: Alexander argues for an underlying and far-reaching interconnectedness based upon fundamental geometrical properties.

findings.antecedent: Damage to fundamental geometrical properties
findings.source: 10. Level three: the transcendent human being.
findings.quote: He also shows how that has been severely, sometimes catastrophically damaged (Salingaros & Masden, 2006b).

findings.antecedent: Transcendent engagement
findings.source: 10. Level three: the transcendent human being.
findings.quote: Much of what we take to be uniquely human, such as our emotions and higher aspirations, is a manifestation of our transcendental engagement.

findings.antecedent: Emotion of love
findings.source: 10. Level three: the transcendent human being.
findings.quote: The emotion of love has throughout the ages generated a strong attachment to other individuals.

findings.antecedent: Love of creator
findings.source: 10. Level three: the transcendent human being.
findings.quote: The love of one's creator anchors our religions, and created the greatest buildings the world has known.

findings.antecedent: Animating aspect of self (filtered by culture and religion)
findings.source: 10. Level three: the transcendent human being.
findings.quote: We connect with our universe through the animating aspect of self, filtered through culture and religion.

findings.antecedent: Abstract ideology
findings.source: 10. Level three: the transcendent human being.
findings.quote: Ironically, they will readily detach themselves from the real world in order to follow an abstract ideology (Hoffer, 1951; Salingaros, 2004).

findings.antecedent: Misinterpretation of science and crude technological applications
findings.source: 11. Architecture that transcends materiality.
findings.quote: The promise of science but a promise based on false premises, eagerly followed by people who did not understand science has over time stripped humanity of some of its most important non-measurable qualities.

findings.antecedent: Non-quantifiable qualities
findings.consequent: Presumption of non-existence, relegation to superstition
findings.source: 11. Architecture that transcends materiality.
findings.quote: What could not be quantitatively measured was presumed not to exist, and was relegated to superstition; a vestige of the past that merited only contempt.

findings.antecedent: Special informational configurations (in physical matter)
findings.consequent: Transcendence of inert materiality, endowment of physical forms with life characteristics
findings.source: 11. Architecture that transcends materiality.
findings.quote: Physical matter does transcend its inert materiality through very special informational configurations. This process can endow physical forms with the characteristics of life: certainly not all of them (i.e., not including metabolism and replication), but moving in a direction towards structures that we identify with living forms.

findings.antecedent: Religious architecture of the past
findings.consequent: Achievement of material transcendence and connective experience
findings.source: 11. Architecture that transcends materiality.
findings.quote: Religious architecture of the past helps us to achieve this type of connective experience; indeed, that was its original purpose.

findings.antecedent: Highest level of human connectivity to material world
findings.source: 11. Architecture that transcends materiality.
findings.quote: When this occurs, the built environment may be said to transcend its materiality.

findings.antecedent: Sacred spaces
findings.source: 11. Architecture that transcends materiality.
findings.quote: Sacred spaces are nourishing to whoever occupies them.

findings.antecedent: Informational fields
findings.source: 11. Architecture that transcends materiality.
findings.quote: informational fields act to establish a manifestation of the requisite connections.

findings.antecedent: Conscious work with informational exchange mechanism
findings.consequent: Re-creation of intensely connective buildings, highest neurological nourishment
findings.source: 11. Architecture that transcends materiality.
findings.quote: Consciously working with the mechanism of informational exchange, we can re-create buildings having the same intense degree of connection. Such buildings will provide the highest level of neurological nourishment.

findings.antecedent: Contemporary religious architecture (without natural elements, figurative art, or ornament)
findings.consequent: Failure to engage user positively, sensory deprivation, physiological unease
findings.source: 11. Architecture that transcends materiality.
findings.quote: Without natural elements, figurative art, or ornament, they fail to engage the user in any positive way. Their empty informational field only communicates sensory deprivation, provoking physiological unease.

findings.antecedent: Natural geometry in living structure
findings.source: 11. Architecture that transcends materiality.
findings.quote: God is manifest in a natural geometry in living structure (Alexander, 2002-2005).

findings.antecedent: Minimalist vs. biophilic geometries
findings.source: 11. Architecture that transcends materiality.
findings.quote: There exists a basic incompatibility between two opposite geometries preferred by human beings.

findings.antecedent: Architects distancing their work from what is natural
findings.consequent: Reliance on artificial criteria and superficial manipulation of images
findings.source: 12. Conclusion.
findings.quote: Architects, on the other hand, in the process of distancing their work from what is natural, have come to rely increasingly on artificial criteria and the superficial manipulation of images.

findings.antecedent: Images and surface effects supplanting everyday human desires and sensibilities
findings.consequent: Humans living in ill-fitting, over-exaggerated, idiosyncratic formal architectural schemes
findings.source: 12. Conclusion.
findings.quote: When images and surface effects supplant everyday human desires and sensibilities in the name of artistic endeavor, humans are left to live out their lives in a series of ill-fitting, over-exaggerated, and often idiosyncratic formal architectural schemes.

findings.antecedent: Architecture turning away from human qualities
findings.consequent: Imposition of building design against human's most basic instincts
findings.source: 12. Conclusion.
findings.quote: Ordinary people see this trend architecture turning away from human qualities as the imposition of building design against their most basic instincts.

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design
findings.consequent: Re-orientation of architecture towards a world governed by coherent information, thinking on many levels of complexity (like nature)
findings.source: 12. Conclusion.
findings.quote: Biophilic design re-orients architecture towards a world governed by coherent information; it also leads people to think on many levels of complexity (which is the way nature works).

findings.antecedent: Various forms of information (calligraphy, representational ornament, abstract geometrical ornament, architectural detail to urban spaces)
findings.source: 12. Conclusion.
findings.quote: The information necessary for humans to connect to the world around them can take many forms, including calligraphy, representational ornament, and abstract geometrical ornament; with the physical object increasing in size from an architectural detail up to architectural structures and urban spaces.

findings.antecedent: Natural and traditional built environments (rich informational content)
findings.source: 12. Conclusion.
findings.quote: The natural and traditional built environments rich in informational content make a place more intrinsically human.

findings.antecedent: Human creations built in coherent manner (like natural world)
findings.source: 12. Conclusion.
findings.quote: The natural world interfaces smoothly with human creations, but only when those are built in the same coherent manner.

findings.antecedent: Emphasizing informational content (in built environment)
findings.consequent: Neurological connection at human scale, emotional nourishment
findings.source: 12. Conclusion.
findings.quote: By emphasizing informational content, we can shape the built environment according to the constituent logic and order necessary to provide neurological connection at a human scale and thus emotional nourishment.

findings.antecedent: Microstructure of natural materials / fine-grained texture/ornament (accessible, fine detail)
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: The smallest perceivable scale is established with either the microstructure of natural materials, or by using very fine-grained texture/ornament. The ordered complexity of natural structure cannot easily be duplicated on this scale. The region containing fine detail has to be immediately accessible to human contact (and not lost at a distance).

findings.antecedent: Inverse-power-law distribution of sizes (many small, few large), articulated texture/ornament (prominent, accessible)
findings.consequent: Ordered detail on smallest scales, fractal connection
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: This rule implies an enormous amount of necessary ordered detail on the smallest scales, just as seen in nature. It also implies the necessity for articulated texture and ornament: not on every surface, but prominent and accessible nevertheless.

findings.antecedent: Definite scaling hierarchy (elements ~3x larger than next smaller, no missing scales)
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: Design that adapts to human sensibilities should have a very definite scaling hierarchy. Obvious differentiated subdivisions or components need to obey a scaling rule, where elements on the next larger scale are roughly 3 times (more accurately, 2.7 times) larger than those on the immediately smaller scale. Although the dimension of each scale can be very approximate so that the ratio between successive scales could be anywhere from 2 to 5, no scale should be missing.

findings.antecedent: Lack of coherent design of intermediate/larger scales (despite natural materials)
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: the intermediate and larger scales have not been designed coherently in recent decades, so the fractal connective effect (which emerges only with the proper scaling hierarchy) is lost.

findings.antecedent: Richness of subsymmetries (smaller/intermediate scales), connective symmetry (across hierarchy), density/interaction of subsymmetries
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: Symmetry is essential in design, not as expressed by an overall scale, but rather by the richness of subsymmetries on smaller and intermediate scales. Connective symmetry is an extensive quality, ideally acting throughout all levels of a scaling hierarchy. The density of subsymmetries, and their intensity of interaction inside a particular scale and across distinct scales, is what leads to visual coherence.

findings.antecedent: Construction hiding materials with informational content (e.g., sheetrock over wood)
findings.consequent: Lack of human connection, abstracted geometry
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: This type of construction hides the materials with the greatest informational content, presenting instead an abstracted geometry to which we cannot connect.

findings.antecedent: Rough stone/brick (hostile to touch)
findings.consequent: Intense informational experience (visual), but negative haptic experience
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: Despite Frank Lloyd Wright's habit of using rough stone and brick for interiors, which at some level do provide a more intense informational experience, their surface is hostile to the touch, thus they should be located out of immediate reach.

findings.antecedent: 'Industrial look' in large buildings
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: there is no connective value in an “industrial look”.

findings.antecedent: Modular production of ornamental panels/components (19th-century, Islamic, Guimard, Sullivan, Wright)
findings.consequent: Effective extension of neurologically-engaging patterns, human wellbeing
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: industrial modules such as those used by Hector Guimard, Louis Sullivan, and Frank Lloyd Wright represent an effective extension of the requisite types of neurologically-engaging patterns... This form of architectural expression contains a high degree of encoded information and is thus very useful for establishing human wellbeing.

findings.antecedent: Natural materials (re-used)
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: Their informational load cannot be duplicated in new materials without incurring a considerably higher cost.

findings.antecedent: Natural unfinished materials, avoiding uniform modular size
findings.consequent: Preservation of material logic, neurological connectivity
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: Another technique is to use natural unfinished materials where appropriate. We should not try to over-control construction by practices such as cutting everything to a uniform modular size... The material logic of these natural materials provides yet another level of neurological connectivity.

findings.antecedent: Concrete (unmanipulated)
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: This is not a natural material, and therefore has to be manipulated before it can give positive sensory feedback.

findings.antecedent: Concrete molded with patterns
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: Instead of letting its surface present either a random texture or an unfriendly flat panel, we can mold it with patterns (as did Frank Lloyd Wright).

findings.antecedent: Unfinished concrete
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: Unfinished concrete has an informationally frustrating surface because it lacks ordered microstructure.

findings.antecedent: Concrete formed with wooden planks
findings.consequent: Lack of visually-coherent surface, unnatural appearance (lacks fractal scaling)
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: using wooden planks to form the concrete does leave a wood grain impression, but this does not produce a visually-coherent surface because it does not have the correct fractal scaling into microstructure, and at best seems unnatural.

findings.antecedent: Craftsmen molding smaller scales of building
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: craftsmen should be given the authority to mold the smaller scales of the building as it develops, so as to foster the most pleasurable feedback as they see it.

findings.antecedent: Individual input in construction
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: By allowing individual input in this manner, we imbue the architecture with a life outside the frozen expression typically conceived on the drawing board.

findings.antecedent: Robotic manufacturing (generating individual components), robotic fabricators emulating material placement variations
findings.consequent: Similar freedom as craftsmen, variability, components/materials endowed with life
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: The same idea can now be implemented via high technology, using computers and robotic manufacturing to generate individual components of a building... We can program robotic fabricators to emulate the variations in the physical mechanics of material placement, so as to endow components and materials with a similar degree of life found in pre-industrial buildings.

findings.antecedent: Repeated identical components (standardized modules)
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: The same degree of life would be impossible to achieve with repeated identical components such as the standardized modules now available for construction.

findings.antecedent: Small part of construction with custom work (using off-the-shelf materials for 95%)
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: this type of work need only constitute a small part of the construction to still provide the desired effect. With just a little imagination, as much as 95% of the materials used could be off-the-shelf materials and standard components.

findings.antecedent: Mathematical coherence (via fractal geometry)
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: The mathematical coherence established through the effective application of fractal geometry elicits the neurological engagement required for a sense of wellbeing.

findings.antecedent: Geometrical interweaving of plant life/natural features, meandering/crenellated building boundary
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: One is geometrical interweaving of plant life and natural features with the fabric of the building itself. We abandon the rectangular or convex footprint of a building, for a more meandering or crenellated boundary that partially surrounds gardens, verandas, and patios.

findings.antecedent: Complex piece of nature (intimate scale, 1-2 meters)
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: Intensify a fairly intimate scale: a complex piece of nature existing on the scale of a human being (1-2 meters in size) can make a substantial difference to our biophilic connection.

findings.antecedent: Native plants (complex geometry)
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: Native plants growing wild define a particular complex geometry, and this is the geometry that can best serve to keep us healthy and make us well.

findings.antecedent: Natural geometry and life on buildings (via weathering, invasion of plants)
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: The development of a natural geometry and life on buildings, via weathering, and via the invasion of plants, is nowadays seen as an unwelcome intrusion as a sign of decay. We, on the contrary, see these as symptoms of increasing life.

findings.antecedent: Urban geometry permitting interaction with nature
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: Human beings can interact with nature only if the urban geometry permits such interactions.

findings.antecedent: Pedestrian access to plant life, designed environment for interaction
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: we need to make it accessible to pedestrians and design an environment in which such an interaction can be maintained and enjoyed.

findings.antecedent: Suburban space (vast expanses of flat lawn and asphalt)
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: The worst disaster is suburban space, in which vast expanses of flat lawn and asphalt define a psychologically-hostile environment for the pedestrian.

findings.antecedent: Suburban layout (exposed sidewalks, forbidden lawns, protective bushes)
findings.consequent: Lack of public realm, poor pedestrian experience
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: Sidewalks are exposed in the middle of this space, between the asphalt road and the forbidden lawn. Private lawns are out-of-bounds, while any bushes and trees form a protective wall around a house, instead of belonging to the public realm.

findings.antecedent: Complex natural areas, diverse green spaces, non-uniform distribution (urban scale)
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: Moving away from large, purely decorative lawns, we try and design many complex natural areas; resisting the amalgamation of every plant into one "park"; resisting the alignment of everything according to a simplistic geometry; and avoiding the homogenization of green spaces to a single plant species.

findings.antecedent: Fractal distribution of green space sizes (many small, few large), internal complexity/variety
findings.source: APPENDIX I: Fourteen steps towards a more responsive design.
findings.quote: A natural (fractal) distribution of sizes applied to green spaces in the city implies the existence of very many small ones, several ones of intermediate size, and only a few large ones. Each of these green spaces should in turn have its own internal distribution, which can be achieved only by having internal complexity and variety.

findings.antecedent: City built radially with green space and farmland fingers
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 3: CITY COUNTRY FINGERS. Build a city radially instead of concentrically, with fingers of green space and farmland coming to its center.

findings.antecedent: Unbuilt land conceived as one whole (farms, parks, wilderness) with access
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 7: THE COUNTRYSIDE. Re-conceive unbuilt land as one whole, encompassing farms, parks, and wilderness, and provide access to all of it.

findings.antecedent: Identification and protection of sacred sites
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 24: SACRED SITES. Identify and protect sites having extraordinary importance to the community, whether they are located in a built or green area.

findings.antecedent: Paving stones and gravel set into grass (for local roads)
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 51: GREEN STREETS. Don't automatically build low-density/low-speed local roads out of asphalt, but instead use paving stones and gravel set into grass.

findings.antecedent: Green spaces (close to living/working, pedestrian accessible)
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 60: ACCESSIBLE GREEN. People will only use green spaces when those are very close to where they live and work, accessible by a pedestrian path.

findings.antecedent: Contact with natural streams, ponds, and reservoirs
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 64: POOLS AND STREAMS. People need contact with natural streams, ponds, and reservoirs, so these must not all be covered up.

findings.antecedent: City accommodating animals (domestic and wild)
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 74: ANIMALS. People need contact with animals, both domestic and wild, so the city must accommodate instead of discourage them.

findings.antecedent: Siting building on least attractive part of lot
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 104: SITE REPAIR. When siting a building, put it on the least attractive part of the lot, preserving the best of the natural environment.

findings.antecedent: Half-hidden garden (not too exposed, not completely hidden)
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 111: HALF-HIDDEN GARDEN. For a garden to be used, it must not be too exposed by being out front, nor completely hidden by being in the back.

findings.antecedent: Shaping buildings around existing trees, planting new trees
findings.consequent: Usable, inviting urban space, social places
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 171: TREE PLACES. Trees shape social places, so shape buildings around existing trees, and plant new trees to generate a usable, inviting urban space.

findings.antecedent: Garden growing wild (according to nature's rules)
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 172: GARDEN GROWING WILD. To be useful, a garden must be closer to growing wild, according to nature's rules, than conforming to an artificial image.

findings.antecedent: Semi-secluded garden seat
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 176: GARDEN SEAT. One cannot enjoy a garden if it does not have a semi-secluded place to sit and contemplate the plant growth.

findings.antecedent: Flowers along frequently used paths (protected, near eye level)
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 245: RAISED FLOWERS. Flowers provide maximum benefit when they grow along frequently used paths; they must be protected and near eye level.

findings.antecedent: Climbing plants on building walls and trellises
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 246: CLIMBING PLANTS. A building connects to its surroundings when plant life grows into it, with the plants climbing up walls and trellises.

findings.antecedent: Paving stones with gaps (allowing growing plants)
findings.source: APPENDIX II: Some patterns from A Pattern Language.
findings.quote: PATTERN 247: PAVING WITH CRACKS BETWEEN THE STONES. Paving stones laid directly onto earth, with gaps between them, allow growing plants to create a half-natural environment.

limitations: The full theoretical and scientific methodology underlying the proposed design steps is too voluminous to be reviewed within the paper.
There is existing confusion on how to actually achieve architectural transcendence in practice.
The paper acknowledges potential criticism from fellow biophilic designers for crossing into philosophy/religion.
Past scientific limitations led to the dismissal of non-measurable human qualities, which the paper aims to re-integrate.
Some past user preference studies were inconclusive or reflected conditioned responses, highlighting the need for physiological measures.

The paper notes a historical disconnect where environmental psychology research was moved out of architectural academia, leading to architects neglecting human physiological and psychological responses.
minimum_safe_summary: This theoretical paper proposes that human beings have an innate biological and neurological need for connection to the natural environment, which is crucial for health and wellbeing. It argues that traditional architecture, with its fractal qualities, hierarchical scaling, and organized complexity, inherently provided "neurological nourishment" by mimicking natural forms and processes. In contrast, modern minimalist architecture, by detaching from these natural principles, creates environments that can cause physiological unease and psychological disconnection. The paper advocates for biophilic design that integrates essential geometrical qualities of nature into buildings and urban structures, emphasizing informational connectivity and a multi-scalar approach to design, drawing on neuroscience to justify these principles and reconnect humans to their built environment. Limitations include the theoretical nature of the propositions and the acknowledged difficulty in translating these complex ideas into practice within current architectural paradigms.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Humans possess an innate tendency to connect with nature and other living systems.
Exposure to natural environments can restore directed attention by allowing for effortless fascination and reducing mental fatigue.
Viewing natural scenes can elicit positive emotional states and physiological relaxation, leading to stress reduction.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper discusses how specific environmental features, both natural and designed, interact with human sensory and neural systems to influence cognitive and affective states, ultimately shaping the human mind and worldview.

steps.from_construct: Exposure to natural environmental features (e.g., views of nature, natural light, fractal patterns)
steps.to_construct: Sensory processing and activation of specific neural pathways (e.g., visual cortex, limbic system, prefrontal cortex)
Modulation of neurophysiological states (e.g., brainwave patterns, neurotransmitter release, autonomic nervous system activity)
Impact on higher-order cognitive functions (e.g., attention, memory, creativity) and emotional well-being (e.g., stress reduction, mood enhancement)

steps.from_construct: Impact on cognitive functions and emotional well-being
steps.to_construct: Shaping of an internally-generated worldview and interaction with genetically-structured neural systems
